Chapter 2. The Weight of Propaganda and the Power of Belief
In North Korea, the line between truth and fiction isn’t just blurred—it’s carefully controlled. From the time you’re a kid, you’re taught to see the world exactly as the state wants you to see it. The leaders? They’re described as loving parents. The country? A paradise, always under threat from enemies. And every bit of progress, no matter how tiny, gets chalked up to the wisdom of those at the top. If something goes wrong, it’s always blamed on outsiders or traitors lurking within.
Picture a young woman—she’s ambitious, smart, and does well in school. She dreams of being a scientist, fueled by stories of the nation’s incredible inventions and heroic workers. Her textbooks are packed with these tales. And why wouldn’t she believe them? She’s never heard anything different. The outside world is just a blank space, filled in only by government warnings and bold boasts.
At home, her family gathers each evening to listen to the news. The reports? They’re always the same. The country is strong. The people are happy. The leaders are wise. But when food runs short, the official story blames foreign enemies for sabotage. If a factory shuts down, it’s chalked up to natural disasters or greedy outsiders. Most folks accept this. Not believing would be unthinkable—it’s just too risky.
But here’s something to pay attention to: belief isn’t always rock solid. Take a doctor working in a small-town hospital. Every day, she treats kids weakened by hunger, and moms desperate for medicine that never shows up. The government brags that their healthcare is the envy of the world, but she knows better—she sees the truth right in front of her. Even so, she keeps her doubts private, sharing them only in whispers with close friends.
The real power of propaganda isn’t just in what it says—it’s also in what it leaves out. The world outside North Korea? It’s painted as chaotic and miserable, but the details are always vague. Most people have never seen a foreigner, never read an international newspaper, never watched a foreign film. And if someone does catch a glimpse—maybe through a smuggled radio or a rare visitor—it usually raises more questions than answers.
Imagine a factory manager struggling to keep things running. He hears rumors about how well things are going in China or South Korea. Are those stories true? He has no way to know, and just asking could get him in trouble. So, he focuses on the job in front of him, finding pride in small victories and camaraderie in shared struggles.
Over time, the line between belief and doubt starts to blur. Most people learn to say what’s expected, to act loyal even if they’re unsure inside. The rituals of propaganda—parades, slogans, official portraits—just become part of daily life. And honestly, it’s often easier to go along with the official story than to face the dangers that come with questioning it.
Still, the human mind is stubborn. In private, people compare stories, whisper their suspicions, and wonder what’s really out there beyond the border. Picture a teenager, restless and curious, listening to a forbidden radio broadcast late at night—heart racing with fear and a spark of hope. Or a mother, quietly worrying about her kids, wondering if there might be a better life somewhere else.
These moments of doubt? They may seem small, but they’re very real. And sometimes, they’re all it takes—a tiny seed of change, planted right in the cracks of a system built on certainty.
